item.description: Tendon-driven continuum robots can reach through constrained spaces, but contact along their bodies is invisible to the sensors at their motors. We show that this is a structural limitation rather than a tuning problem: the map from contact forces to tendon measurements has a null space of dimension at least seven, so no estimator that leaves the contact support free can locate contact. When the obstacle geometry is known, however, non-penetration and complementarity make the contact force locally identifiable, and we prove that the resulting system with unknown contact inputs is locally exponentially strongly detectable. We present a constrained moving horizon estimator (MHE) that encodes these conditions and runs in real time as one quadratic program per sample, and we give a local, mode-wise robust stability result for it. In a finite- element benchmark of a two-section robot pressing and sliding on a wall, the estimator located contact to 0.9 mm and estimated contact force to 0.22 N, compared with 65 mm and 0.72 N for a tuned extended Kalman filter (EKF) with state projection. The estimator tolerated millimeter- level errors in the obstacle position and unmodeled wall friction, under which the projected EKF failed. Under randomized model mismatch over 40 trials, including unmodeled tendon friction, it remained better in force and location in every trial. Without contact, the MHE offered no advantage over the EKF, which confirms that its benefit comes from the contact constraints. This report extends a letter submitted to IEEE Control Systems Letters with complete proofs and additional experiments.

item.title: How far does a hash-only sender go? A pre-registered map of sender memory versus bits for short text messages
item.description: Can a sender that only computes hashes, with a language model only at the receiver, transmit short human text more cheaply than a classical sender trained on the same domain? We answer with one pre-registered run on 1,000 English user utterances from Taskmaster-1. The primary endpoint is the cost per message to deliver 100% of the messages (hash bits, plus a 2-byte negative acknowledgement and the raw text when the first attempt fails), paired against an in-domain PPM order-1 sender. The hash-only sender delivered 857 of 1,000 messages on the first attempt and cost 192.8 bits per message, 18.4 bits more than PPM order 1 (95% bootstrap interval 10.9 to 26.3); by the pre-registered rule it spends more and is not equivalent within one byte. As secondary results we map measured sender memory against bits. The hash-only sender (8,190 B on a host build, keyed BLAKE2b tag included, as in every method) was the cheapest point in bits from 8,190 B up to, but excluding, PPM order 1 at 24,844 B, 45 to 46 bits below smaz2 and Unishox2; from PPM order 1 upwards, in-domain senders spend fewer bits, except order 2 pruned to 16 KiB. In airtime it loses to PPM order 1 on all five links priced, to Unishox2 on four, and to raw text with a tag on two, because each failure costs an acknowledgement frame and a fallback frame. A wider receiver search recovers half of the failures and makes the cost 7.7 bits lower than PPM order 1, at about three minutes of receiver time per failure, and still loses in airtime on four of five links. We report the measurement as a delimitation, with every deviation of the run.

item.title: Beyond Prompt Attacks: Least-Action Auditing of Concept Erasure
item.description: Concept erasure, or concept unlearning, in text-to-image diffusion models is usually audited with prompt attacks. A prompt attack tests whether one conditioning string still retrieves the erased concept. It does not measure the probability that the frozen generator still assigns to that concept. We introduce least-action auditing of this residual probability, and evaluate it on Stable Diffusion concept-erasure checkpoints. The least-action barrier is the minimum control cost of driving the frozen reverse process into a detector-defined concept event. This cost equals the path-space KL divergence of conditioning the model on the event, and therefore the event's negative log-probability. The estimate $ΔS_{\mathrm{rob}}$ uses a CLIP$\wedge$DINOv2 consensus terminal, with no retraining and no adversarial prompt. Across $18$ erased concept-mechanism pairs spanning object classes and NSFW nudity, $ΔS_{\mathrm{rob}}$ predicts deployment leakage counted on $1{,}500$ fresh samples per model by detectors excluded from the audit (pooled Spearman $ρ{=}{-}0.76$, $p{=}5{\times}10^{-4}$). Within every audited concept, the eraser with the higher barrier leaks less ($18/18$). On NSFW nudity the barrier orders the standard erasers exactly: UCE $ΔS_{\mathrm{rob}}{=}3.9$ (leak $16.4\%$) $<$ ESD $75.5$ ($9.8\%$) $<$ RECE $224.5$ ($1.4\%$), while Safe Latent Diffusion (SLD) stays near zero and leaks $85.5\%$ under explicit prompts. The same trajectories repair deployed checkpoints. An audit-guided closed-form patch reduces UCE nudity leakage from $16.2\%$ to $0/1{,}500$ and RECE church leakage by $3.3\times$, where direction-count-matched random edits fail.

item.title: The Cost of Coverage: Conformalising Native Forecast Uncertainty for GB Wind Power
item.description: Uncertainty bands on wind forecasts help inform reserve sizing and commitments, but often fail to deliver their stated coverage. We apply conformal prediction to native bands to see what it adds and what it costs, comparing six forecasters, from ARIMA to a tabular foundation model, at two wind farms in Great Britain (GB) under operational conditions. We show that calibration repairs empirical marginal coverage with little or no Winkler Score penalty, but this apparent success conceals under-coverage in high winds. Calibrating by forecast wind regime turns marginal coverage into regime-level coverage, cutting day-ahead out-of-band volume in high winds by over 40% relative to pooled calibration while narrowing bands overall.

item.title: A proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture
item.description: Aaronson and Ambainis conjectured that every bounded polynomial of low degree on the discrete cube has an influential variable. They showed that the conjecture implies that the acceptance probability of every quantum algorithm making $T$ queries can be approximated on most inputs by a classical algorithm making $\mathrm{poly}(T)$ queries. We prove their conjecture: every function $f\colon\{-1,1\}^n\to[-1,1]$ of degree at most $d\ge1$ has a variable of influence at least $c\,\operatorname{Var}(f)^{5/2}/d^{6}$, where $c>0$ is an absolute constant. In the original formulation, for polynomials of degree at most $d$ with values in $[0,1]$ on $\{0,1\}^n$ and variance at least $\varepsilon$, this gives a variable of influence at least $(\varepsilon/d)^{7}$. The proof is elementary, with steps inspired by works of others. Thus, as Aaronson and Ambainis anticipated, superpolynomial quantum speedups in the query model require structure, such as a promise on the inputs.

item.title: Autonomous Code Review: Hidden-Test Results on GitHub Issues
item.description: Can an autonomous cross-provider review step change whether code written for a real issue passes hidden tests? We report a retrospective benchmark of 12 historical GitHub issues (five C#, five JavaScript, and two Python) from five repositories. Two directed author--reviewer pairs, OpenAI GPT-6.1-Sol and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5, each ran twice per issue, yielding 48 planned workflows. A bounded terminal agent produced an initial patch; a cross-provider model reviewed it; the author model adjudicated findings and could revise the patch. The same hidden evaluator assessed initial and final patches. Forty workflows completed, while eight terminated before a complete evaluator outcome. Four completed workflows passed, and all four already passed before review. No initial-to-final pass/fail transitions occurred among completed workflows.

item.title: Verifier Noise Is a Temperature: Testing Tilt Predictions in Finite-Budget LLM-Guided Search
item.description: LLM-guided search loops propose a modified candidate, score it, and keep it if it scores better. When both candidates are re-scored at every comparison, as in the minibatch acceptance gates of prompt optimizers, keep-if-better is a reversible Markov chain if the score difference is logistic and the mutation operator is reversible, and its stationary law is the mutation equilibrium tilted by exp(beta f). For any continuous symmetric noise difference the same tilt is the stationary law of a small-step diffusion limit, with beta = 4F'(0); for a minibatch gate beta grows with the square root of the minibatch size. Caching the incumbent's score instead inflates the recorded score. We test the tilt as a prediction for LLM-guided program search, committing each prediction from calibration data before the search runs. The level after 150 steps rises with the minibatch size in six of seven settings, but its predicted value fails: on bin packing, search attains 62-88% of the predicted gain when the proposer edits the parent and 109-119% when it writes new heuristics. The attained fraction falls with the parent-child quality correlation of unselected mutation; a registered test on two new settings confirmed the direction, but not the quantitative agreement after a correction. Further registered tests found that runs started from a good program kept losing quality over 300 steps, more so from starts that search had selected, by a margin that passed its registered rule narrowly. Runs from different starts had not reached a common level, so whether the tilt describes the stationary law of LLM editing remains open. A registered test in prompt optimisation on frozen task-model scores failed: search exceeded the tilt, and the bin-packing relation did not transfer.

item.title: Real-Time Self-Penetration Repair for Skinned Characters with Soft Contact Budgets
item.description: Motion that is plausible on one body can penetrate another after a change in shape, and motion models can produce self-penetration on their native characters. We present a training-free post-process that reduces these artifacts through pose correction followed by bounded skin compression. The module attaches to any motion model whose native character and output character have compatible character packs, without access to model internals. Each pack is built offline from the rig and skin without training. A vertex-level pose layer solves a local quadratic program in plain C on one CPU core, and a stateless contact deformer acts on the host's final skinned mesh. A part-dependent soft-tissue budget allocates correction between pose and skin through a static convention. Source penetration contributes no extra allowance; optional cloth thickness and compliance modify the pose layer's collision surface. Operation is causal or uses a short buffered lookahead, with frame-exact pass-through at the native interface for clean, inactive frames in the zero state. Across 320 unseen clips and 3 body shapes, the fraction of frames with hand-torso depth above 20 mm falls from 15.53% for copied motion to 0.00%, with final maximum depth 9.3 mm over every frame. Mean pose and skin costs are 1.11 and 1.18 ms, respectively, and their sum of 2.29 ms is a sub-frame processing cost. The median joint-velocity high-frequency ratio relative to copied target motion is 1.008.

item.title: From Function Inversion to Preimage Reporting
item.description: Given an arbitrary function $f:[N]\to[M]$, the function inversion problem asks to preprocess $f$ and to be able to, when given some $y\in [M]$, decide whether there exists some $x\in [N]$ such that $f(x)=y$ and if so, to report such an $x$. Recently, Fiat-Naor's solution to this problem has seen significant traction in theoretical computer science, and allowed for several conjectures related to meta-complexity and the 3SUM problem to be broken. In this paper, we consider the natural extension of the function inversion problem that we call preimage reporting. Here, instead of having to report only one $x\in [N]$ such that $f(x)=y$, the whole set $f^{-1}(y)$ must be found. We present a new general method to convert any arbitrary function inversion scheme into an efficient corresponding preimage reporting scheme. In particular, if $Δ$ is the maximal indegree of $f$, we show that we can perform preimage reporting using space $S$ in time $T$ for any $T$ and $S$ satisfying $TS^2=N^2 Δ$, matching a variant of a tradeoff obtained by Fiat and Naor for function inversion. This last result implies an improvement over the corresponding function inversion scheme itself, which constitutes the first function inversion scheme whose query time is inversely proportional to $|f^{-1}(y)|$. We derive new simple solutions for the $k$SUM-indexing with reporting and Jumbled indexing with reporting problems.

item.title: Parallel Algorithms for Higher-Order Temporal H-Index Computation
item.description: Ranking vertices by importance is a fundamental task in network mining. The H-index provides such a ranking by asking how many neighbors are themselves well connected; its higher-order temporal variant recursively applies this idea over time-respecting neighborhoods in temporal networks. Scaling its computation is difficult because the existing streaming algorithm intertwines temporal processing with H-index order, incurring maximum-degree-dependent costs and exposing little parallelism. We show that the temporal dependencies can instead be resolved once: each edge's time-dependent lookup is mapped to a fixed successor position, turning every H-index order into a parallel gather followed by a segmented suffix-H computation. Based on this reformulation, we derive a linear-work suffix-H algorithm, a parallel multicore CPU implementation, degree-adaptive GPU kernels, and a multi-GPU scheme that exchanges only distinct remotely queried states. Experiments on synthetic and real-world temporal graphs show that the reformulation alone is substantially faster than the streaming algorithm, and that GPUs add order-round speedups exceeding an order of magnitude over our multicore implementation on synthetic inputs with up to one billion temporal edges. On a 636M-edge Reddit network, eight GPUs compute 128 orders in 3.6 s of round time, whereas the streaming algorithm does not finish within an hour even at order 8.

item.title: Capacity of Generic Symmetric Distributed Linear Computation: The Geometry of Relations
item.description: In distributed linear computation, $K$ users observe linear functions of common finite-field data and send separate messages to a server that wants another linear function. We characterize the generic capacity $C$, the minimum total number of field symbols sent per computed instance, when all observations and the demand have dimension $ν$, the data have dimension $μ$, and the coefficients of these linear functions are drawn independently and uniformly from the field and stay fixed during coding, with the field size growing through arbitrary prime powers. For fixed $K$, $C/ν$ depends only on $τ=μ/ν$: the curve has finitely many linear pieces for at most three users, infinitely many pieces approaching one value of $τ$ for four users, and a rational part between two sequences of linear pieces for five or more users. The geometry of the relation space, formed by the linear relations among the observations and the demand, determines three things: the shape of the curve, which relations the coding scheme aligns, and the entropy inequalities used in the converse. Generically, the user subspaces of this space are either balanced, where the capacity lies on a single rational curve, or split into two balanced components, a sparse and a dense one, which produces the linear pieces. Achievability uses asymptotic set alignment, in which monomial precoders confine the combined observation differences to a small set. The converse uses the same geometry to lower-bound the sum of the users' remaining observation entropies in terms of the remaining data entropy.

item.title: Entering a New Domain in the Era of Generative AI: An Autoethnography of Solo Game Development as a Bioinformatics Educator
item.description: The rapid improvement of generative AI (GenAI) not only increased the efficiency of practice but also empowered individuals with capabilities to explore new domains. However, identity formation in the wake of such empowerment remains understudied. We use an autoethnography to understand identity formation in the context of solo game development as a bioinformatics educator. With the goal of developing a create-your-own-adventure (CYOA) game, we collected data for 73 days through journal entries, interacting with communities of practices. The autoethnographer had continuously reassessed the situation, and closely interacted with communities of practice. Their prior knowledge was used to provide in-game context and to uniquely interpret game development processes. These findings suggest that the autoethnographer made efforts to belong to communities of practice and engaged extensively in sensemaking through the lens of a bioinformatics educator. Although GenAI puts power at hand, attaining a new identity took place at a human pace.

item.title: On Positive Computation
item.description: We introduce new notions of reducibility for monotone classes and show that a monotone version of Circuit Satisfiability and the Hamiltonian Cycle Problem are complete for $mNP$, even under positive reductions (which are not the same as monotone reductions). If this holds for all (monotone) $mNP$-complete problems - that they are also so complete for $mNP$ -, then $P\neq NP$. We introduce positive models of relativized computation and show that the separation $posP\subsetneq mNP$ does not relativize, even when oracles are restricted to monotone sets. Yet, there is a (weak) diagonalization proof that $posP\subsetneq mNP$.

item.title: Half-precision inference of AI weather prediction models: negligible loss of skill at a fraction of the cost
item.description: AI weather prediction models are released with 32-bit (fp32) weights and run in fp32 by default, although current GPUs compute much faster in 16-bit formats. We run five publicly available models -- Aurora, Pangu-Weather, FourCastNet, SFNO and FastNet -- on a single 16 GB GPU from 52 initial dates in 2024, in fp32 and with their networks in half precision (fp16), and verify the forecasts against ERA5. The physical state must stay in fp32: converting the whole model rounds it in physical units, which in fp16 overflows and in bf16 discards meaningful information. With the state, its normalisation and denormalisation in fp32, running the network in fp16 changes the global RMSE by at most 1.4%, and by about 0.5% or less for four of the five models, equivalent to less than one hour of lead time up to day 8 and at most two hours at day 10. The differences show no systematic pattern by region, scale or for tropical and extratropical storms, apart from a small tropical penalty in FourCastNet, and fp16 leaves the CRPS, spread and calibration of Aurora's ensemble almost unchanged. No value overflowed fp16's numeric range (+/-65,504); the largest stay 38 to 544 times below it. A 10-day forecast in fp16 is 1.3-3.5 times faster than in fp32 and uses 1.4-3.7 times less energy. Sensitivity experiments show that rules of thumb from other applications of reduced precision carry over only partly: the first and last layers dominate for some models but not for others, and no type of layer is sensitive on its own. For running AI weather models on a single GPU, fp16 with the state in fp32 is practically lossless at a fraction of the cost. bf16, often preferred for its wider range, is as fast but less accurate than fp16 for every model, and simple 8-bit quantisation costs far more skill.

item.title: CID: Measuring Cognitive Work Through Semantic State Change
item.description: Traditional information theory provides powerful tools for analyzing statistical properties of information but offers limited insight into meaning and semantic transformation. It has never been possible to quantify the meaning of an arbitrary piece of information. Large language models represent information as vectors embedded within high-dimensional semantic spaces, enabling meaning to be analyzed geometrically. This paper defines semantic state as the vector representation of information within a model's semantic space and defines cognitive work as the transformation between semantic states, movement through semantic space. To quantify this transformation, we introduce the Contextual Information Differential (CID), a covariance-aware metric based on Mahalanobis distance measuring semantic displacement relative to the structure of the embedding manifold. By treating meaning as a geometric property of semantic space, CID provides a practical method for measuring semantic change, cognitive transformation, and information processing. This framework establishes a foundation for analyzing cognitive processing, learning, reasoning, knowledge generation, synthetic expertise, and human/AI collaboration through implementation-independent measurement of semantic state change in both human and artificial systems.

item.title: Multimodal Training with Knowledge Traction for Video Anomaly Detection
item.description: The task of weakly supervised video anomaly detection is challenging. Existing approaches mainly model video frame features and determine whether anomalies are present based on their magnitudes. In this work, we propose a novel method that incorporates external knowledge into training to improve model performance, robustness, and generalization. We leverage textual prompts and a large language model (LLM) to establish prior information for the specific task, and employ dictionary learning to normalize and compress this information. Moreover, during experiments, we observed inconsistencies in the textual descriptions extracted from similar video frames by image caption models. To address this, we devise a method that leverages an LLM and auxiliary information to ensure consistency in the textual descriptions of similar frames within a video. Finally, we introduce a feature processing approach that incorporates prior knowledge and cross-modal attention mechanisms. This approach learns the relationships and characteristics among different modalities to construct more accurate and reliable feature representations, thereby improving the accuracy and stability of downstream tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses other state-of-the-art approaches.

item.title: Memory as a Temporal Resource: Lifetime Contracts for Multi-Retention Systems
item.description: Computers move and rewrite data whose useful lifetimes range from inner-loop iterations to years, yet memory systems usually hide retention as a fixed physical property. We argue that required lifetime should become a first-class resource across algorithms, programming systems, controllers, and devices. Building on prior lifetime-aware placement, we propose an event-based validity contract that links application completion events to retention-class selection and renewal of protection. Applications would be enabled to express semantic contracts such as ``until this tile completes'' and the system will map data to homogeneous arrays engineered for ephemeral, epoch, or durable retention and preserve correctness through margins, ECC, refresh, migration, or recomputation. We present a trace-based simulator and FPGA prototype that exercises class migration.

item.title: Benchmarking Speaker Embedders in the Sub-Second Regime for Real-Time Voice AI Agents
item.description: Real-time Voice AI agents must separate the active user from intelligible background speech that survives conventional noise suppression. Background sources include television audio, family members, and colleagues. Production denoisers remove non-stationary environmental noise effectively. Background speech shares the spectral characteristics of the target and passes through, causing false acceptances in downstream speaker verification (SV) and automatic speech recognition (ASR). We benchmark open-source speaker embedders TitaNet-Large, TitaNet-Small, ECAPA-TDNN, CAM++, and SpeakerNet under a strict sub-second latency budget. Evaluation combines a controlled benchmark with a weighted human-annotated production set. Our controlled benchmark is built from real calls in which a second real speaker is injected into silence intervals at modulated amplitude. We report three findings. First, denoising before embedding is generally harmful and raises equal error rate (EER) across architectures. Second, truncating audio below the full voice-activity segment degrades every model. Third, roughly half of the TitaNet embedding is redundant for this task. Trailing dimensions encode population attributes such as language and gender. Such attributes carry little discriminative value in a demographically homogeneous user base. We distill these results into deployment guidance. Verification should run on raw audio with full voice-activity chunks. Thresholds should favor precision over F1. Truncated embeddings reduce the cost of similarity search.

item.title: Additive $Ω(\log^* OPT)$ Gap for Bin Packing with Three Items per Bin
item.description: We prove that bin packing is NP-hard to approximate within an additive factor of $o(\ls\OPT)$, even when all item sizes are arbitrarily close to $1/3$. This gives the first lower bound for bin packing with an additive factor that depends explicitly on the optimum value. In addition, we give a polynomial-time reduction from any bin packing instance into one with item sizes arbitrarily close to $1/3$, preserving its additive configuration-LP gap up to constant factors. Thus, in the sense of additive configuration LP gap and up to a constant, we confirm the conjecture that 3-partition instances are the hardest bin packing instances. In particular, we obtain an unconditional $Ω(\ls\OPT)$ gap for 3-partition instances. We build on the recent OpenAI construction that uses five items per bin and rules out any constant additive gap.

item.title: A Spiking Neural Model of the Mental Lexicon: Representations, Similarity Structure, and Associative Retrieval in Perception and Production
item.description: A neural account of lexical access requires an explicit distinction between the structure of lexical representations, the associations linking representational levels, and the activity generated during retrieval. This paper specifies a spiking neural implementation of the mental lexicon within the Neural Engineering Framework and Semantic Pointer Architecture. Conceptual and phonological form representations are constructed recursively from relational graphs, whereas lemma representations provide independent lexical identities. The implementation contains 613 lexical entries and supports two directed processing pathways: perception maps a phonological form to its associated concept via a lemma, whereas production maps a concept to its associated phonological form via a lemma. Each pathway combines two associative-memory variants, winner-take-all (WTA) selection (competition) and thresholded transfer, and uses 199,400 leaky integrate-and-fire neurons. We formalize within-level similarity, cross-level associative retrieval, and the interpretation of decoded activity. Simulations show successful retrieval of eight selected words from the lexicon in both processing directions, with retrieval evaluated against all 613 lexical entries. These simulations use complete phonological forms as input for perception and complete concepts as input for production, illustrating lexical retrieval through the corresponding processing pathways. This paper provides a transparent description of lexical representations and neural retrieval mechanisms, supported by accessible code, lexical data, and online simulation documentation.

item.title: Precedence Constraint Scheduling on a Fixed Number of Machines
item.description: We give a deterministic exact algorithm for $P_m\mid\mathrm{prec},p_j=1\mid C_{\max}$ for every fixed $m\ge3$. The algorithm constructs an optimum schedule in $$ O(L)+m^{O(m^2)}\, n^{6m^2+13m+1} \, {\log n} $$ elementary RAM operations, where $n \ge 2$ is the number of jobs and $L$ is the binary input length. Its word size is $O(m^2 \log n)$ bits. An implementation with a fixed number of tapes uses $O(L)+m^{O(m^2)} \, n^{12m^2+26m+2} \, \log^3 n$ steps. For three machines the respective polynomial degrees are $94$ and $188$, apart from the displayed logarithmic factors.

item.title: Against All Likelihood
item.description: Maximum likelihood is the dominant training principle for large language models, yet likelihood is neither necessary nor sufficient for truth. Unlikely events happen every day, and frequently repeated statements can be false. Drawing on a philosophical tradition that ties objectivity to invariance rather than probability (from Nozick's account of objective facts and Wigner's principles of invariance to the structural realism of Poincaré and Cassirer), we argue that the truth of a statement should be judged not by its probability under a single distribution, but by its invariance across relevant transformations of the environment. We connect this view to machine learning literature on out-of-distribution generalization and invariant learning, sketch how invariance could be tested at inference time with language models, and discuss implications for continual learning.

item.title: Pairwise Reconnection for Cost-Distance Steiner Trees
item.description: The Uniform Cost-Distance Steiner Tree Problem asks for a rooted tree that minimizes the connection cost plus a weighted sum of root-to-terminal distances. We develop an algorithm that constructs two candidate trees: one based on direct connections to the root and another that pairs selected vertices and connects each pair to the root. The algorithm selects the tree with the smaller objective value. The resulting randomized algorithm achieves expected approximation factors of $1.698$ in the spanning case and $2.041$ in the general case, and it can be derandomized in polynomial time. The pairwise matching analysis charges part of the augmentation cost directly to the connection and delay costs of an optimal solution, rather than only to the separated lower bound used in previous analyses. This allows the $1.698$ factor to fall below the maximum multiplicative gap of $1+1/\sqrt{2}$ between the optimum value and that lower bound. We give instance families with approximation-ratio lower bounds approaching $1+1/\sqrt{2}$ for cut-and-reconnect algorithms that start from a minimum spanning tree and $3/2$ for the present algorithm. Finally, we show that the Uniform Cost-Distance Steiner Tree Problem and the Steiner-tree version of the Cable-Trench Problem are approximation equivalent up to an arbitrarily small additive loss.

item.title: Open-world Reconstruction-based Classifier with Concept Drift Adaptation
item.description: Data stream processing has become central to modern machine learning applications, with concept drifts and novel class appearances posing the primary challenges faced by recognition methods. Adapting to concept drifts while also being able to detect novel classes and distinguish groups of unknown observations can be seen as a step towards effective method employment in an open-world setting. This work proposes a classification method that can detect and learn the distributions of new, unknown classes, as well as adapt to concept drifts once the distribution of known classes shifts. The proposed method uses the autoencoders' reconstruction errors and the KDE that models their distribution. The autoencoders incrementally adapt to the changing distributions of known classes via weight fine-tuning, resulting in continuous adjustment to evolving concepts. Conducted experiments used a diverse set of synthetic data streams, embeddings of a real-world static CIFAR dataset arranged into a stream to simulate concept drifts and the emergence of unknowns, as well as real-world datasets where novelty is observed. The methodology was compared with state-of-the-art approaches with three-criterion recognition quality assessment and resource consumption evaluation. The results indicate that the proposed method is competitive with reference approaches in stationary environments and performs best when concept drifts occur.

item.title: Orthogonal Norm Growth in Two-Tower Retrieval: A Popularity Mechanism for Unified Discovery
item.description: Unified search and recommendation systems may update the same item vectors from both interaction streams. We study how repeated updates can increase an item vector's norm and affect retrieval under an unnormalized dot product. A cosine-only loss makes the output gradient perpendicular to the current item vector - tangent to its constant-norm sphere. Training changes encoder parameters, however, so the realized item-vector movement need not remain tangent. We derive sufficient conditions under which it does; every nonzero update then increases squared norm by its squared length. When the tasks share an item encoder, sequential updates from both can accumulate in the same norm, which raw-inner-product serving can expose for either task. This conditional result is not a theorem about joint SGD. Controlled ablations test these conditions. On MovieLens 32M and Amazon Books, accumulated tangent movement accompanies frequency-norm association and additional head-item exposure under raw-dot rather than normalized-item ranking. In a nonlinear tower combining a per-item ID vector with a shared content encoding, active item movement remains near-tangent. We separate its norm change into the ID-update contribution and other output changes, then use a matched training intervention that removes immediate norm growth caused by the ID-row update. The intervention reduces norm-related exposure but also recommendation utility, so it is diagnostic rather than a proposed mitigation. Our logs are recommendation-only: the formulation supplies a shared-representation audit, while prevalence in joint traffic remains open.

item.title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming Across a Difficulty-Graded Ladder of Two-Player Games
item.description: Weight-space programming sets every weight of a feed-forward network by hand, from an explicit specification of the desired computation, with no gradient descent and no training data anywhere in the construction. We ask how far a large language model can carry this practice, zero-shot, across games of deliberately increasing difficulty. We design a four-rung ladder (Nim, tic-tac-toe, two sizes of Connect Four, and a chess endgame) spanning four axes of difficulty, and build a second, independent network at each rung, using a structurally unrelated game at matched difficulty, to separate what a rung's finding says about the difficulty level from what it says about the one game used to measure it. Ten networks are built and independently verified. Six admit a complete, non-statistical proof of correctness against an independent oracle. The chess-endgame rung is exact where correctness is cheap, move legality and, in one network, an exact one-ply mate detector, and collapses where it is expensive, composing a multi-move mating plan, from 84.1-100% success at the one-ply tactics it was built to get right down to 0.57-9.13% in full adversarial play; its replicate shows this collapse is an order of magnitude less severe under a shorter required plan and exact rather than heuristic safety checks. The standard-sized rung confirms, by holding hand-set evaluation weights fixed and adding only shallow search, that the remaining gap is an architectural ceiling rather than a matter of engineering effort, and this exact collapse reproduces across two structurally unrelated games. We release all ten networks, their independent oracles, construction-cost measurements, and a cold-prompt protocol for a future cross-model comparison

item.title: Forecasting cumulative intraoperative hypotension burden: patient-disjoint evaluation of quantile boosting and alert policies
item.description: Background: Binary hypotension forecasts do not describe the depth and duration of future low pressure. Burden forecasts may support graded early warning, but better forecast scores need not yield more useful alerts. Objective: To evaluate conditional quantiles of the next 15-minute mean arterial pressure (MAP) deficit below 65 mmHg and distinguish forecasting performance from episode-warning performance. Methods: Public VitalDB numeric arterial MAP was reduced to 10-second medians without forward filling. Subject-disjoint training, validation and test splits included 70,402, 14,270 and 15,575 labeled windows. We compared climatology, calibrated persistence, last-MAP-only boosting, and direct and residual quantile boosting, with and without additional MAP-history features. Patient-weighted pinball loss and subject-bootstrap intervals evaluated forecasting. Validation selected alert thresholds before a hash-recorded test evaluation. Results: In the test split, the prespecified residual-versus-persistence comparison at the 90th percentile yielded losses of 2.256 and 2.900 mmHg-min, respectively (difference -0.644; 95% interval -0.814 to -0.487). Direct prediction achieved 2.196, and direct prediction with additional MAP features achieved 2.193. Episode-warning results were sensitive to the alert rule and operating threshold. Conclusions: This retrospective benchmark separates burden-forecast skill from warning-policy performance. Findings support further study of direct burden estimation; they do not establish patient benefit, prospective reliability or transportability beyond the source hospital.

item.title: Representational drift in a code model: behaviour settles, which neurons carry it does not
item.description: In neuroscience, representational drift is a change in which neurons carry a representation while behaviour stays the same; we measure its analogue in OpenCoder-1.5B during pretraining, for 169 Python constructs over two trillion tokens at a constant learning rate, with a noise unit on every change, at checkpoints as close as 1,000 training steps. For 16 of the 169, those whose grammar fixes a next token, the loss at those positions reaches its floor within the first 4% of training, while the model's reliance on the neurons carrying them grows to the end: removing them costs 0.06, 0.25 and 0.40 nats more than removing a random set, at 4 billion, 84 billion and 2 trillion tokens. Which neurons carry a construct never settles: for all 169 the carrier set is still changing at the last checkpoint, and an abrupt settling at any date from 84 billion to 1.5 trillion tokens, or a gradual one before 500 billion, would have been detected in 99% of injected cases. The set measured at 84 billion tokens, removed at the end, cannot be separated from a random set, so the function is carried by whichever neurons are current. Up close the change is a persisting pool and a changing sample: a neuron that leaves a construct's set returns at three times the rate of a matched neuron, and no set reassembles. The hypothesis we fixed in advance, that the carriers settle, is refuted; we discuss candidate causes and name the experiment that would separate them.

item.title: Calibrated concept profiles: making the reading of a model's neurons a measurement
item.description: Interpretability has largely moved from reading a model's neurons directly to reading a second model trained on the first: a probe, a sparse autoencoder, a crosscoder. The move answered real faults -- mixed meanings, thresholds without a unit, readings that did not transfer from one study to the next -- but gave up what a direct reading alone provides: nothing trained in between, the neurons themselves named, and a reading that can be repeated and compared. Here the direct reading is made a measurement. A neuron's activation varies with the prompt, so its reading is a distribution over a population of stimuli. We declare that population: every factor around a target construct is drawn at its rate in a reference corpus and logged. From the declared distribution we generate a battery of prompts, and draw it twice. From the battery we compute the calibrated concept profile, one number per neuron, stated in units of the neuron's own spread on ordinary input; the two draws give every number a noise unit. Before the profile is read, a fixed set of checks licenses the battery on the model, and the smallest change the profile can resolve across training checkpoints is measured. Realised for Python on OpenCoder-1.5B and followed across checkpoints spanning two trillion training tokens, the profile gives what the alternatives do not report: a unit on every number, a chance level for every comparison, and which neurons carry a construct at every checkpoint. The battery, the code and the data behind every result are released.

item.title: RoleWalk: training-free structural embeddings for directed graphs that transfer across graphs
item.description: Structural role embeddings describe a node by its position in a graph - hub, bridge, periphery, member of a dense core - rather than by who its neighbours are. Existing methods either learn coordinates specific to one graph (struc2vec, Role2Vec, RESD) or read scales and normalisations from the whole graph (GraphWave, Digraphwave), so the same neighbourhood can receive different coordinates in two graphs; few read edge directions. We present RoleWalk, a training-free embedding that follows a short lazy random walk from each node and records, at each step, two distributions: that of the transition probabilities, through its characteristic function at a fixed grid of frequencies, and that of the walker's distance to its starting node. On directed graphs, walks that go forward then backward add who shares a node's targets or sources. The embedding depends only on a node's neighbourhood within a fixed radius, so its coordinates mean the same thing in every graph. We show that, without curvature, it is the kernel mean embedding of the walk's footprint, that it separates graphs that the Weisfeiler-Leman test cannot, and that pruning small probabilities comes with a per-node error certificate. Empirically, RoleWalk is competitive with the best role embeddings on five classification benchmarks at a fraction of their cost, has the highest scores on real directed roles in Wikipedia adminship, exceeds the published accuracy of Digraphwave at every noise level of its own Enron network-alignment benchmark, transfers centrality predictors to graphs four times larger better than existing inductive embeddings, hand-made features and a trained GIN, and embeds a million nodes in 20 s to 3 min on one CPU core. The code is open source (BSD license): https://github.com/kerighan/rolewalk

item.title: Language, Not Code Abstraction: Natural-language Training Shapes Brain-aligned Geometry
item.description: Code-trained language models produce positive brain scores, which raises the question of whether abstract structure learned from programming languages can substitute for natural-language training. We trained 25 GPT-2-small models on TinyStories, Python, C functions, x86-64 assembly, and the corresponding machine code, and scored them using a shared tokenizer and encoding procedure against matched random-weight models. On Pereira-243 and Tuckute2024, TinyStories exceeds the mean of the four code models by $Δr = 0.053$ and $0.059$ (Holm-corrected $p<0.001$), while code training leaves alignment near the random-weight level. The language advantage is benchmark-specific: Blank2014 shows no corrected language-code difference, and Fedorenko2016 shows no language benefit. Geometry tracks the encoding result on Pereira-243: TinyStories seeds converge on the most similar representations, and its fit-free correspondence with neural dissimilarity peaks at $ρ= 0.14$, twice the code and random-weight levels. Binary-trained models have about three effective dimensions, so seed agreement alone does not imply neural correspondence. Updating only the embedding matrix on English improves mean-over-depth alignment for every code model more than an equal update on its own corpus. Within this architecture and training setup, natural-language training produces a distinct representational geometry with closer neural correspondence on Pereira-243

item.title: Reconfiguration of Time-Bounded Descriptions
item.description: Time-bounded Kolmogorov complexity measures a string by the length of its shortest program that prints it within a deadline. An adjunction-universal machine (Bauwens, Kozachinskiy, and Shen, arXiv, 2025) is a Turing machine that simulates every Turing machine $M$ on every input $z$ with polynomial overhead when given a code of $M$, computable from $M$ in polynomial time, followed by $z$ unchanged. Any two adjunction-universal machines give the same measure up to an additive constant and a polynomial change of the deadline. However, this measure records only the shortest program for a string. We study all programs of one length that print a string within one deadline, join two of them when they differ in one bit, and ask when this graph is connected. Fix any adjunction-universal machine. For almost all $m$-bit strings and every deadline beyond some polynomial, the graph is disconnected at program length $m+O(1)$ and has at least $2^{m-O(1)}$ components at length $2m+3$. In contrast, we build an adjunction-universal machine in which every such graph is connected or empty, at every deadline, once the program length reaches a computable threshold that is at most exponential in the length of the string. Exponential thresholds are unavoidable: for every adjunction-universal machine with such thresholds and every large $m$, more than three quarters of the $m$-bit strings need a threshold exponential in $m$. For our machine, above the threshold, every program for the string is within three bit flips of a connected set of fastest programs for the string, along a path inside the graph, at every deadline by which that program halts. For this machine, deciding whether two given programs are connected in this graph is $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete when the input is the string, the deadline in unary and the two programs; for each fixed string it takes polynomial time.

item.title: Seeing vs. Counting: Complexity Twins Show Where Multimodal LLMs Fail on Diagrams
item.description: When a multimodal LLM miscounts in a diagram, does it fail at seeing or at counting? Existing visual graph and puzzle benchmarks vary visual density and algorithmic hardness together, confounding the two. We pair counting questions about the same drawing that sit in different counting-complexity classes, such as its spanning trees (a determinant) and its simple paths (#P-complete), and use a transcription probe and a text-only control to separate reading from computing. We test Gemini, Gemma and Qwen3-VL models; for the Gemini models, the answer depends on how the model computes. In chain of thought, most of them read small drawings correctly and then fail at counting, at a rate set far more by the size of the answer than by its complexity class (for the primary model, the odds of an exact answer fall 2.38-fold per decade of the answer). Given code and an exact transcription, the primary model counts correctly even on 10x10 grids, and reading becomes the bottleneck: a single view misses horizontal edges, and a second reading of a rotated copy with crop checks reads 86/96 large grids exactly, against 57/96 when the upright reading is simply repeated.

item.title: Calibrating your confidence requires thinking of all the ways you could be wrong
item.description: A primary limitation of modern deep learning is the miscalibration of model confidence; traditional architectures fundamentally lack a mechanism to quantify their own uncertainty. Larger models and larger datasets mitigate this issue, but they do not resolve the underlying structural deficiency. Bayesian methods offer a principled uncertainty-aware learning framework through stochastic parameters. Yet, despite the established benefits, the inherent computational overhead often compromises either scalability or quality. This trade-off currently prevents the widespread adoption of Bayesian methods. This Thesis bridges the gap between high-quality and low-complexity by introducing a novel distribution on parameter space: a degenerate Gaussian whose covariance is a projection matrix aligned with the null space of the Fisher information matrix. We demonstrate the scalability of this Bayesian posterior through two numerically efficient algorithms: one for posterior sampling and another for the direct computation of predictive confidence. Empirically, we show State-Of-The-Art confidence calibration and out-of-distribution detection for large models. We provide theoretical grounding for this approach. We study the degeneracies inherent in Amari's information geometry and highlight its most relevant component: the split of parameter's perturbations into two orthogonal subspaces. From this perspective, our posterior naturally emerges as the simplest choice that captures this split, assigning unitary variance to one subspace and zero variance to the other. Moreover, through the tools of differential geometry, we utilize this split to identify and rectify a critical misalignment issue of the non-linearized Laplace Approximation. Finally, with a focus on PAC-Bayes generalization bounds, we pave the way for a deeper understanding of the learning capabilities of overparametrized models.

item.title: Same Facts, Different Remedy: Linguistic Profiling and Arbitrariness in LLM and System One Decisions
item.description: Large language models are increasingly used to resolve consumer complaints, and the way complainants write varies with age, education and socioeconomic status (SES). We audit three remedy-decision systems using sociolinguistic rewrites of US consumer financial complaints that are instructed to preserve every fact: two generative LLMs that return a single label (GPT-4o-mini and GPT-5-mini) and a probabilistic "System One" model that returns a distribution over remedies (Jev). Using pre-registered hypotheses tested once on held-out complaints, we separate two phenomena that single-label audits conflate. At the group scale, older, college-educated and higher-SES styles receive slightly more generous remedies; these effects replicate but are small, with every monetary-remedy gap within 0.5 percentage points. At the individual scale, two style versions of the same complaint receive different monetary decisions 2.6-6.3% of the time. In a variance-component analysis of the probabilistic model, persona components shared across the two rewrite models account for about 1.6% of within-complaint variation. The persona gaps are associated mainly with delivery (vocabulary, grammar, politeness) rather than content. Positive controls show that all three systems respond 49-387 times more strongly to remedy-relevant facts than to style. Rewriting every complaint into one standard style reduced GPT-4o-mini's education and SES gaps by 94% and 87% while retaining fact sensitivity, but reversed two of the probabilistic model's gaps and did not make individual decisions more stable. Independent LLM auditors flagged material fact changes in 3.3% and 11.7% of rewrites, and instability persisted among unflagged rewrites. Fairness audits of LLM decision systems should report group disparities and individual instability as separate outcomes.

item.title: The Drawing You Watch Is the Portrait You Keep: A Replayable Machine Portrait Studio
item.description: Ask an image model for your portrait and a finished picture arrives: no first line, no second thoughts, no record of how it got there, and a different picture if you ask again. I built a portrait studio that works the other way. A sitter chooses one of eight fictional artists, each written with a city, a medium and a tempo of its own, holds still for 8 to 12 seconds, and watches a drawing of themselves appear over 44 seconds. One still is sent after consent, a hosted image model returns a private study the sitter never sees, and a compiler turns that study into one drawing document. The live drawing, the saved sheet, the vector export and the film all read that document, and a replay makes no model call, so the drawing you watch is the portrait you keep. I describe the compiler in enough detail to rebuild it and say plainly what it is: an authored reconstruction at a compressed speed, not a recorded hand. On 16 generated test studies a sheet holds 8,784 to 16,378 timed contacts, about three quarters of them fixed-grid fills and nearly all shorter than one video frame, and recompiling one study gave byte-identical output four times on one machine. The paper also traces a bug that matters more than any of that. The earlier compiler estimated the paper colour tile by tile, read dark skin as paper, and in all eight hands kept less of a deep-complexioned face than a fair one (13 to 48 percent against 41 to 56). On 80 generated studies the rebuilt engine keeps the complexion difference the study already has (raw retention 89 to 120 percent), so the fairness question has moved upstream, to the study and the hosted model. The two test sitters are generated and differ in more than complexion, and no real-face or perceptual study exists yet. The studio is live at https://everyfaceproject.com.

item.title: VLA Handover: Failure-Prediction-Based Switching from On-Robot to Server VLA Models
item.description: Large vision-language-action (VLA) models generalize well but are difficult to run in real time on a robot, and small VLAs that run there fail more often. Remote inference over beyond-5G and 6G networks lets a robot use a large VLA on a server, but querying the server for every action chunk limits the number of robots per server. We propose VLA handover: the robot runs a small VLA (S-VLA) and switches to a large VLA (L-VLA) on a server only when the S-VLA is likely to fail. We formulate the switching as minimizing the request cost under a required success probability and, since this problem cannot be solved directly, propose a heuristic framework that retrains neither VLA. In simulation with SmolVLA and $π_{0.5}$ on three of the four LIBERO suites, VLA handover raised the success rate by 11-22 percentage points over the S-VLA alone and sent 49-77% fewer requests than server-only control at a 2-4 percentage-point lower success rate, and its completion time grew less with the network latency.

item.title: Stabilizing Vector Approximate Message Passing with Circuit-Designed Lag-Lead Damping
item.description: Vector approximate message passing (VAMP) often fails to converge on ill-conditioned matrices, and its damping factor is tuned either manually or adaptively. Using the fact that VAMP iterations are the discretization of an electric circuit, we show that the denoiser and the likelihood act as nonlinear resistors, the Onsager correction is a mirror resistor and damping is a lag filter. This circuit gives a closed-form loop gain whose spectrum can predict when VAMP fails. Because a lag filter cannot isolate the oscillating modes, we add a lead capacitor whose design often results in a negative capacitance. Across a wide range of condition numbers, our proposed damping strategy achieves a higher convergence rate than adaptive damping and Anderson acceleration at a lower mean iteration cost. On ill-conditioned multipath channels, across ranks and sparsity levels, it also converges more reliably than existing damping baselines.

item.title: Using an LLM to Tackle Difficult Cases in NER for Nepali Tweets
item.description: Named entity recognition (NER) is challenging for social media data in a low-resource language. LLMs often lag behind pretrained language models (PLMs) in NER performance, but they show promise in handling cases that PLMs struggle with. Using a dataset of Nepali tweets, we split the test set into "easy" and "hard" cases using token probabilities from a fine-tuned pretrained language model (PLM). We then evaluate an LLM on the hard test cases using 16 different prompt configurations. We find that selecting examples based on semantic similarity and increasing the number of examples improves F1 score by almost 10 points from the baseline configuration. Although the LLM underperforms the PLM on the full and easy test sets, it surpasses the PLM on the hard test set, resulting in an improved score when the two models are combined.

item.title: Global Sinkhorn Convergence and Spectral Stability of Matrix Scaling
item.description: We give a global spectral bound for the Sinkhorn--Knopp (SK) algorithm. Let $A$ be a row-stochastic nonnegative $n\times n$ matrix admitting a finite doubly stochastic scaling $B$. Define \[ g=1-s_2(B)^2>0, \qquad D=\min\left\{\|(u,v)\|_\infty: B=\operatorname{diag}(e^u)A\operatorname{diag}(e^{-v})\right\}. \] From the standard initialization, SK achieves total marginal $\ell_1$ error $\varepsilon$ in \[ O\!\left(\frac{D+\log n+\log(1/\varepsilon)}{g}\right) \] iterations. A scale-invariant potential contracts globally according to the spectrum of $B$. The linear dependence on $D$ is necessary in the fixed-gap regime: we construct strictly positive inputs with constant input and endpoint spectral gaps, $D=Θ(n)$, and an $Ω(n)$ iteration lower bound at error $n^{-2}$. Our upper bound gives $O(n)$ iterations on this family. We next give spectral certificates for scalability and short scaling distance. For a row-stochastic input $A$ with positive column sums $c_j$, set \[ K=\frac{\max_jc_j}{\min_jc_j},\qquad σ=s_2\!\left(A\operatorname{diag}(c)^{-1/2}\right). \] The input-only condition $\sqrt K\,σ<1$ certifies exact scalability and polynomial scaling distortion, with $D=O(\log n)$ for fixed $K$ and a fixed positive spectral margin. Given a finite scaling $B$, the weaker condition $\sqrt K\,σs_2(B)<1$ gives the same structural bounds. With a constant endpoint gap, these bounds imply logarithmic SK iteration complexity. Boundary constructions show that the strict spectral inequalities cannot uniformly be replaced by nonstrict ones.

item.title: Richness Is Not Evenness: Ordered Renyi Crossings under Self-Training
item.description: Recursive self-training of language models, a setting studied in model collapse, can reduce vocabulary while making frequent words, mostly function words, less dominant. We fine-tune English GPT-2 on its own output for nine generations, vary the training-data sampling temperature, and measure every model with one fixed sampler. As training temperature rises, Renyi entropy changes turn from loss to gain at distinct temperatures: min-entropy first, then collision entropy, Shannon entropy and observed richness. Between the outer crossings, word types fall while the most-common word becomes less dominant. Untruncated training at T = 1 lies in this interval: at 13,000 words, generation 9 has 24% fewer types than generation 0 yet collision entropy is 0.91 bits higher. The ordering persists with a finer grid, different measurement samplers, a fixed word budget and five fresh training seeds. Min-entropy again crosses before richness in four further settings (in Hindi only at interpolated roots) and in 12 of 13 distinct measurements under eight text representations. Next-token identities and a categorical simulation isolate decoding and sampling effects; the crossing order remains empirical. Fine-tuning on human text can produce the same split while likelihood improves, and no single order's sign reliably identifies worse likelihood across the tested settings. We recommend reporting entropy profiles at stated budgets with an independent quality measure.

item.title: Quantum Interactive Proofs of Proximity
item.description: We initiate the systematic study of quantum interactive proofs of proximity (QIPPs). These are quantum interactive proof systems with sublinear communication, where the verifier accepts inputs in a property $Π$ and rejects inputs $\varepsilon$-far from $Π$, while only querying the input a sublinear number of times. 1. We show that all logspace-uniform $\mathbf{NC}$ properties admit QIPPs with query, communication and time complexity all $\widetilde{O}(n^{2/5})$. This improves on the best known classical total complexity of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt n)$, which is optimal in the worst case for polynomial-time verifiers under the PRG assumption of Kalai and Rothblum (CRYPTO, 2015). This resolves an open question of Dall'Agnol, Gur, Roy Moulik, and Thaler (Quantum, 2022) in the affirmative. 2. Assuming the existence of a post-quantum subexponentially secure PRG computable in logspace-uniform $\mathbf{NC}$, we prove that, for every nondecreasing, logspace-computable query bound $q(n)\le n^{1/2-Ω(1)}$, there exists a property $Π$ in logspace-uniform $\mathbf{NC}$ and a constant $\varepsilon>0$ such that no polynomial-time $\varepsilon$-QIPP for $Π$ can achieve query complexity $q(n)$ and communication complexity $c(n)$ satisfying $q(n)+c(n)=o(n^{1/3})$. 3. We establish a bi-directional connection between QIPPs for logspace-uniform $\mathbf{NC}$ and query-model QIPs for parity. A QIP for $k$-bit parity with total complexity $k^{2/3-Ω(1)}$ yields QIPPs for every logspace-uniform $\mathbf{NC}$ property with total complexity $n^{2/5-Ω(1)}$. Conversely, achieving total complexity $o(n^{2/5})$ within the standard $\mathsf{PVAL}$-based framework requires improving the known query-communication tradeoff for parity. Additionally, we show that almost every size-$2^{βn}$ property ($0<β<1$) requires linear total QIPP complexity at constant proximity.

item.title: Learning Whom to Trust About the Unseen: Source Credibility and Reliability Transfer in Language Models
item.description: A source who has been right before deserves attention, but about what? We ask how far a demonstrated record of reliability travels in language models when the new claim cannot be checked, and whether the answer depends on the kind of claim. Three behavioral studies across six models approach the question from three angles. Study 1 adapts the Einstein-effect paradigm and finds that models, unlike the human sample, favor a spiritual leader over a scientist for the same obscure statement, and that the preference largely reverses when the statement is reworded in the vocabulary of physics. Study 2 adapts a paradigm in which a trusted expert calls a scientific or religious explanation unknown or a mystery; models reproduce the human domain asymmetry in exaggerated form. Study 3, the central test, gives two fictional informants different records on checkable river forecasts and then has them endorse matched claims about hidden natural and spiritual causes of the same village events. Most models carry the record to natural causes and barely at all to spiritual ones; one model transfers it weakly to either. Telling the model that the reliable informant forecasts by spiritual guidance rather than by measurement lowers that informant's influence on natural claims in every model and produces no comparable gain on spiritual claims in any. Demonstrated reliability thus has a scope in these models, and the account a source gives of how they came to be reliable can narrow it. Whether this reflects a judgment about relevance or the low prior credence of spiritual claims is the question the design leaves open, and we outline the experiment that would settle it.

item.title: Hardness of Approximation for Polynomial Optimization over Sphere for Linear Programming Relaxation Hierarchy
item.description: Semidefinite programming (SDP), particularly the sum-of-squares (SoS) hierarchy, provides $n^{O(q)}$-time approximation and certification algorithms for optimizing degree-$d$ homogeneous polynomials on the unit sphere. For arbitrary inputs, degree-$q$ SoS gives a powered-objective approximation factor $O_d((n/q)^{d/2-1})$ [BGGLT17]. For random order-$d$ tensors, degree-$d$ SoS has an integrality-gap lower bound of $2^{-O(d)}(n/d)^{d/4-1/2}$ relative to the true spherical maximum; lower bounds also extend to growing SoS degree in tensor PCA [BGL17,HKP17]. We establish lower bounds for weaker linear-programming relaxation hierarchies. Our degree-$q$ moment LPs impose the sphere identities and any prescribed, instance-independent family $\mathcal{G}$ of valid polynomial inequalities of degree at most $q$. They include Sherali--Adams-type product hierarchies. For every even $d\ge2$, constant $C>0$, and $q$ satisfying $2d | q$ and $2d\le q\le n$, every such relaxation with at most $n^{Cq}$ tests has instances $P$ satisfying \[ \frac{\mathrm{PowLP}_{q,\mathcal{G}}(P)}{\|P\|_\infty}\ge \frac{c_{d,C}}{\sqrt{q\log n}}\left(\frac nq\right)^{d/2-1/2}.\] Here $\|P\|_\infty$ is the maximum absolute value of the polynomial over the sphere and $\mathrm{PowLP}_{q,\mathcal{G}}(P)$ is the relaxed objective. The exponent $d/2-1/2$ improves the leading dependence on $d$ relative to the $d/4$-type exponents in prior random-tensor SoS lower bounds. Our LP hierarchies impose weaker positivity conditions than semidefinite moment relaxations. It leaves open whether analogous degree dependence can be achieved in lower bounds for SDP hierarchies.

item.title: The Matthews Correlation Coefficient: Fifty years
item.description: Fifty years after its introduction, the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) remains central -and debated- in binary classification. This survey offers a comprehensive retrospective and an in-depth analysis of MCC, covering its historical development, mathematical foundations, and implications for practice. We clarify long-standing misconceptions, formalize its equivalences (to Pearson's correlation and to Chi2 in 2x2 tables), and examine its behavior under class imbalance. Beyond MCC, we develop analytical (derivatives) and graphical (contour plots) frameworks that generalize to any confusion-matrix-based metric. These frameworks expose structural properties -bias, robustness, sensitivity- that scalar summaries conceal, and they provide actionable guidance for selecting and interpreting performance measures in applications where reliability and fairness matter. Together, our results position MCC within a broader toolkit while clarifying when it is informative -and when alternatives may be preferable.

item.title: AircraftWitness: How Often Aircraft Can Locate Recordings
item.description: Aircraft overhead can reveal where an outdoor recording was made. Propellers and rotors leave Doppler curves in audio, and public ADS-B archives log equipped aircraft. We measure how often, blind and against chance. Our main test was registered and timestamped before any audio, and its two amendments came before any answer was read. It covers 24 new places, with the recorders' own clocks, a 300 s slack and a 20 km square. The best of three locators places clear-pass clips within 1 km at 4 places, where a uniform guess predicts 0.57 (p = 0.0065 after correcting for the pick). With the wrong time or swapped audio it places none. The other two hit 1 and 2. On 360 clips from 7 places of a GPS-timed network, two locators place 6% and 8% within 1 km. By place, a unit chosen after that run, they hit 4 and 5 of 7 where a uniform guess predicts 2.3. On 1,600 random public recordings, picked and cut without the truth in a time-bounded run, the three locators answer at most 20 times and place at most 2. We release AircraftWitness, a benchmark, and pass labels for 11.7 million recordings.

item.title: Jacobian-Causal Memory Control for Persistent Memory in Language Model Systems
item.description: Persistent-memory systems choose not only which records are retrieved but which prior information can alter current inference. We propose Jacobian-causal memory control (JCMC), which represents each authorized memory intervention by a predicted influence signature in a shared behavioral measurement space, selects interventions against a target effect and side-effect budget, and compares predicted with observed effects before retaining or rolling back the intervention. Under explicit smoothness and bounded-estimation assumptions, we prove a quadratic local-approximation bound, characterize the target effects reachable by a set of signatures, bound selection regret under signature error, and bound non-additive interactions between simultaneous memories. The paper reports no benchmark measurements; it defines a paired counterfactual estimator and an evaluation protocol comparing JCMC with relevance, graph, and policy-filtered retrieval baselines. The central claim is narrowed or falsified if those simpler baselines match effect targeting, side-effect control, and rollback utility under equal model, memory, policy, and cost budgets.

item.title: Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS): A Formal Mathematical Framework
item.description: Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) operates on document pairs, returning a single scalar per comparison. In a multi-document setting where several sources may have contributed to one or more targets, pairwise STS cannot disentangle each source's marginal semantic contribution from their shared vocabulary. In this paper, Semantic Conditional Similarity (SCS) is introduced as a conditional form of STS that computes similarity between two documents after eliminating semantic elements shared with a third via set-theoretic operations. SCS makes four contributions: 1) it introduces directionality, partitioning pairwise relations into lateral (inter-source) and vertical (source-to-target) classes; 2) conditioning induces role-dependent asymmetry by extending the comparison domain from unordered pairs to ordered, conditioned triples of a target, a reference, and a conditioning document; 3) SCS introduces inter-document conditioning by subtracting shared content from a third document, complementing the intra-document conditioning in recent C-STS work; and 4) the set-theoretic decomposition achieves threshold-free partitioning of shared and residual content, requiring no arbitrary similarity cutoff. Although developed for the $n \to 1$ configuration, the framework extends to $1 \to n$ via vertical role reversal and to $m \to n$ via independent composition of source- and target-side conditioning. With the established $1 \to 1$ case, these span the full spectrum of document cardinality. SCS scores should be interpreted ordinally, as rankings of marginal contributions rather than absolute measurements. The broader implication is that metric space axioms commonly assumed in similarity formalizations constrain expressiveness in role-differentiated multi-document settings, and that extending the domain to conditioned triples can recover information that pairwise-symmetric comparisons suppress.

item.title: Gain-Dependent Entropy Characterization of a Zener Avalanche Noise TRNG via Dual NIST Standards: Toward Low-Cost Hardware Entropy for ICS Deployments
item.description: True random number generators based on Zener avalanche noise offer a low-cost entropy source for industrial control system and IoT edge devices, yet the relationship between amplifier gain, coupling capacitance, and entropy quality remains uncharacterized under current NIST standards. This paper presents a comprehensive entropy assessment of an op-amp-based Zener avalanche noise generator across five gain configurations and two coupling capacitor values, evaluated against the NIST SP 800-22 statistical test suite and the SP~800-90B entropy source assessment using 1.44 billion raw bits per configuration. We identify a three-phase autocorrelation structure, attributed to comparator saturation-recovery dynamics, consistent across all gain settings. A direct-current substitution experiment, replacing the Zener diode with a stable voltage source at the same bias point, reduces switching activity by approximately 97%, confirming that Zener avalanche noise, rather than amplifier self-excitation, is the necessary entropy source. The coupling capacitor is further shown to govern comparator overdrive and entropy quality independent of this source mechanism, with the smaller capacitance improving entropy, throughput, and bias. The combined results identify an optimal gain configuration achieving a perfect statistical test score, NIST-compliant min-entropy, and peak entropy throughput at a bill-of-materials cost under five dollars, offering practical design guidance for low-cost entropy sources in industrial and embedded deployments.

item.title: ReKV: Overlapping Quantized KV Transfer and Suffix Recomputation
item.description: Prefill--decode disaggregation moves a prompt's key--value (KV) cache between workers before the first token can be generated. Reducing this handoff to either cache compression or recomputation misses a useful choice: which layers to transmit, at what precision, and which layers to execute again on the decode worker. ReKV transfers a quantized prefix KV cache and one BF16 boundary state, then reconstructs a contiguous suffix while the prefix is in flight. In a model-shaped synthetic benchmark on cross-node H100s, the Q8 configuration meeting separately evaluated quality criteria reduces 8K handoff latency by $2.36\times$, $2.84\times$, and $3.65\times$ over BF16 transfer for Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen2.5-3B, and Qwen3-8B. It is also faster than the best measured transfer-only or recompute-only action at those points. A separate real-weight BF16 recomputation experiment reduces prefill-to-token-return time by $1.16$--$1.63\times$. The preferred action changes with prompt length and link bandwidth.

item.title: AlterNet: Adaptive-Depth Mixture-of-Experts with Learned Halting for Elastic Inference
item.description: Most LLM architectures have fixed compute demands determined at training time. We propose a novel architecture that combines the Mixture-of-Experts architecture with shallow experts and a novel dynamic-depth system to make the extent of a forward pass dynamically adjustable. Our approach lets the model automatically determine the compute needed for a given task, paired with a system to scale it down after training without retraining when the execution environment demands faster or cheaper inference. To achieve this, we introduce an iterative computation mechanism, sequence-level depth-based routing steered by a halting mechanism within the experts, a depth encoding that lets the model track its progress in the chain, and a regularization mechanism that incentivizes the model to use allocated compute efficiently. We present initial benchmarks and discuss future research directions.

item.title: Faster Treasure Hunt via Strongly Universal Exploration with Polylogarithmic Overhead
item.description: We study deterministic exploration and delayed-activation treasure hunt in anonymous undirected port-labeled graphs with incoming-port information. From polynomial-time constructible ordinary universal exploration sequences of length \(O(n^c)\) for a fixed regular degree, we construct a single infinite strongly universal exploration sequence with cover time \(O(n^c\log^2n)\). Summable dyadic insertion schedules yield the sharper bound \(O_\eps(n^c\log n(\log\log n)^{1+\eps})\) for every fixed \(\eps>0\), together with refinements at every fixed iterated-logarithm depth. The proof combines reversible excursions, neutral guards and an arbitrary-window argument that treats both orientations simultaneously. For this recurrence, uniform linear expansion is equivalent to convergence of the normalized period sum. Exact counting identities also permit direct instruction access. With a logspace ordinary generator, table-free enumeration of decreasing scale paths computes instruction \(t\) using \(O(\log(t+2))\) working bits and time polynomial in \(t\). The earlier polynomial-slack bounds follow as corollaries. A local cubic simulation extends the treasure-hunt application to arbitrary-degree graphs, with the \(2m\)-vertex replacement size included explicitly in the bound.

item.title: Turkish Multimodal Video Fact-Checking: A New Dataset and a Comparison of Zero-Shot Agentic and Fine-Tuned Systems
item.description: Video-based misinformation spreads rapidly on social media, but almost all existing fact-checking systems focus exclusively on English text. Tools for low-resource languages such as Turkish are severely limited. In this work, we present TeViD (Turkish Video Fact-checking Dataset), to the best of our knowledge the first multimodal video fact-checking dataset for Turkish. We compiled the dataset from articles published by Teyit.org, an IFCN-certified organisation, and enriched it with translated Snopes articles and synthetic examples to reduce class imbalance. Building on TeViD, we develop two verification pipelines that share the same open-source base model. First, in 3MFact-TR (Pipeline 1), we adapt the multi-role 3MFact framework to Turkish with the Qwen2.5-7B large language model and the Qwen2-VL-7B vision-language model, and add three modules of our own: a semantic inconsistency checker, a 5W1H question manager, and a bilingual evidence retriever that excludes fact-checking sites to prevent leakage. Second, as our Fine-Tuned Model (Pipeline 2), we fine-tune a single Qwen2.5-7B with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to produce closed-book verdicts from the claim and the video's textual description. We report accuracy, macro F1, True class F1, and True class recall for both systems, together with ablation studies.

item.title: SPRING-5: Measuring Tool Documentation Repair for LLM Agents by Efficiency
item.description: Methods that repair tool documentation automatically are mostly evaluated on task accuracy. We report a benchmark that scores them on cost. SPRING-5 is 20 tool families and 344 tasks, each with a deliberately degraded specification, a hand-written honest one, a deterministic backend and an answer key, scored on calls charged against the ideal call path. A wrong answer is charged the full call budget, so this cost index largely tracks the completion rate, and we report calls per correct task beside it, which carries no such charge. Over 2,644 baseline sessions, 54% of wrong answers arrive with no rejected call, no refusal and no retry. The benchmark carries three validity instruments. A build-time ceiling assertion requires the honest specification to reach the ideal path and fails systematically on only one family. A dud rule names the families a stronger model solves cold and catches four. A directly measured noise floor shows that two evaluations of a byte-identical specification differ by a 95% factor of 0.64 to 1.56, so about one comparison in eight crosses a conventional win threshold on noise alone, and the cheap way of estimating that floor is biased by which families happen to go unedited. Against these instruments, a schema-only method closes 1% of the baseline-to-ideal cost gap, an online self-evolution loop 13%, one batch rewrite over every training transcript 33%, and a variant given correctness labels 58%. The batch advantage over the loop is the evidence it reads: held to the loop's exposure it is no longer detectable. With five and ten tools in context the effect survives, the baseline cost does not change, and only machine-written descriptions sent calls to the wrong tool.
